Clara needs a wedding dress. The wedding is in June. She has come to a shop in Charlottenburg with Mara, her maid of honour, and with Lena.
Good afternoon! Are you the bride? Congratulations! What kind of dress are you looking for?
Something simple. I don't like big dresses with lots of lace.
Then I'll show you the modern styles first. Here, the long silk dress, or the short one with wide sleeves.
Mara, what do you think? The long one or the short one?
Try on the long dress first. The white silk goes well with your red hair.
And then the short one. The short dress is more practical if you're celebrating on the beach.
We're celebrating on the Baltic Sea, in Kiel, in my parents' garden. Right by the water.
Wow. Clara. You look wonderful. The long dress is perfect.
But the low back… Isn't it a bit too sexy for your grandmother?
My grandmother? My grandmother got married in 1968 in a short red dress! She'll love the low back.
And a veil? We have the short one here, or this long lace one.
No veil. On the beach it'll just blow away anyway. I'll take the long dress. No veil. And with comfortable shoes!
The ending -en is pronounced short and weak: “den neuen Mantel” ≈ “dayn NOY-en MAN-tel”.
Kleid, Seide, weiß = “eye”; but Schleier = “SHLY-er”, Spiel = “shpeel”.
“schlicht” = “shlikht”: sch + l + i + soft ch + t.
1. The adjective after the verb vs. before the noun
After the verbs sein, werden, bleiben, the adjective does NOT change: “Das Kleid ist weiß.” But when the adjective stands BEFORE the noun, it takes an ending: “das weiße Kleid”.
The coat is new. → the new coat
The woman is old. → the old woman
The word order is the same as in English: the adjective comes BEFORE the noun. “the white dress” = “das weiße Kleid”. The difference: in German the adjective takes an ending.
2. The endings after der / die / das
After the definite article, the adjective has only TWO possible endings: -e or -en. The article already shows the case, so the adjective has “little work to do”.
The easy rule: -e in the five boxes in the top-left corner (nominative singular + feminine and neuter accusative). Everywhere else: -en.
In the plural and in the dative: always -en. “mit den bequemen Schuhen”.
3. The same endings after dieser, welcher, jeder
Words that end like the definite article (dieser, welcher, jeder, alle, mancher) use the same adjective endings:
This long veil is made of lace.
Which white dress are you taking?
Every new colleague gets a key.
All the young people are dancing.
When it's clear what we're talking about, the adjective can stand on its own, with its article and ending:
The long one or the short one? (das Kleid)
I'll take the blue one. (den Anzug)

Adjectives used as nouns (with a capital letter): der Alte (the old man), die Kleine (the little one), das Neue (the new thing), “etwas Schlichtes” (something simple), “nichts Besonderes” (nothing special).
Colours: hellblau (light blue), dunkelblau (navy blue), hellgrün, dunkelrot… The colours “lila”, “rosa”, “orange” are usually not declined in everyday speech.

While Clara was finding her dress, Jonas had a different problem. He needed a suit. Jonas had never worn a suit, not even at his own confirmation, because back then he had worn his father's old leather jacket, much to his mother's annoyance.

He went on his own to a big department store at Alexanderplatz. An hour later he came back empty-handed. The black suits were too sad, the blue ones too boring, the grey ones too old-mannish, and the light beige suit the young shop assistant showed him made him look “paler than a patient after an operation”.

The next day he went with Clara to a second shop, a small, expensive one in Charlottenburg. There he tried on a dark green suit, which actually suited him. But when he saw the price on the small white label, he went a little green himself. “Eight hundred euros,” he whispered. “That's more than our whole wedding cake.” Clara laughed so loudly that the elegant shop assistant raised her eyebrows. They left the shop without a suit, but in a very good mood.

During the coffee break on ward 4, he told Mara about his problem. Mara thought for a moment and said: “I know someone who has a good suit. A very good one. And who has the same build as you, just fifty years older.”

On Saturday, Jonas was standing in Ludwig's flat, under the yellow lamp. Ludwig opened the big old wardrobe in the bedroom. It smelled of lavender and of time. Right at the back, in a grey plastic cover, hung a suit.

This is my wedding suit. 1974. Navy blue, pure wool, from a little tailor's shop on Schönhauser Allee. The old tailor was called Mr Kowalski. He worked on it for three weeks. Ingrid said I looked like a film star in it.

Jonas put on the navy blue suit. The jacket fitted perfectly at the shoulders. The trousers were a little too short, but only by two centimetres. Mara and Ludwig looked at him and said nothing for a long time.
Jonas, you look like a film star. A film star from the seventies, but a film star.
Mr Brandt, I can't accept it. It's your wedding suit. It's too precious.
Lad, this suit has been hanging in the dark wardrobe for fifty years. A beautiful suit doesn't want to hang in a wardrobe. A beautiful suit wants to dance. And Ingrid would have said the same.

Then Ludwig took a little box out of the top drawer. Inside was a narrow tie, dark red with little gold dots. “The right tie,” he said. “Ingrid chose it. She said: a blue suit without a red tie is like a sky without the sun.”

Jonas tied the red tie, slowly, because he didn't know how. Ludwig helped him with his right hand, which was healthy again now. The old fingers made the knot quickly and surely, as they had fifty years ago.

Ludwig told the story while he tied the knot. The wedding in 1974 had been small, at the registry office in Prenzlauer Berg, with twenty guests. Afterwards they had celebrated in the courtyard, this very courtyard, under the same chestnut tree, which was much smaller back then. Ingrid wore a short white dress that her sister had sewn for her, and the band “The Rails” played until two in the morning, without its guitarist, because the guitarist was dancing with the bride. The neighbours had made potato salad, and a former colleague from the transport company had brought a tram bell. Every time the young couple kissed, he rang the bell.

There was just one problem left: the trousers that were too short. But the building had a solution for that too. Mrs Hoffmann could do more than play the piano. In the hard years after the war she had sewn with her mother to earn money for piano lessons. “Bring me the blue trousers,” she said on the phone, “and a good lamp. My old eyes are weaker than my old hands.”

Two days later, the navy blue suit was hanging in its grey cover again, this time in Jonas's flat in Friedrichshain. The trousers were exactly two centimetres longer. In the lining of the jacket, Mrs Hoffmann had embroidered something in fine gold thread, so small that you could only see it if you were looking for it: “L & I 1974 · J & C 2027”.

When Jonas discovered it, he rang Mara straight away. He could hardly speak. “Tell Mrs Hoffmann thank you,” he said at last. “And Mr Brandt. And tell him the old suit is going to dance again. I promise.”

Mara passed on the message. Ludwig said nothing. He just nodded, went to the window and looked for a long time at the chestnut tree in the courtyard, where the first green leaves were growing. Then he picked up his guitar and played the song he had danced to with Ingrid in 1974. Fritz lay down on his feet and listened. Outside in the courtyard, spring was slowly arriving.
